question: Where is the industry heading on fee structures and pricing transparency?

claims.text: Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, Feb 2025): McKinsey says that after fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, citing PriceMetrix by McKinsey. Fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships have stayed at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.

Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, April 2026): McKinsey writes that it expects repricing of services where clients perceive no differentiation, such as basic tax projections. It calls the fear of an immediate, industry-wide fee freefall "likely overstated" because planning is usually embedded in a broader advisory fee. It believes fee pressure will manifest as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
Position - fee pressure will be uneven, not a blanket cut (McKinsey, April 2026): The same piece ties pricing transparency and unbundling directly to the expected form of fee pressure.

Position - asset-based (AUM) fees remain the core model (survey research): The Kitces wellbeing study (published 2023-12-20) found 79% of responding advisor teams primarily derive client revenue from AUM fees. Another 10% were retainer-oriented, and the remainder were divided largely between hourly fees and commissions. Cerulli (published 2025-05-28) found 33% of affluent investors say they compensate their provider via an asset-based fee and 36% prefer it. It also found 21% use a no-fee platform and 20% a commission-based method. Cerulli's analyst says firms should not limit themselves to one engagement option.

Position - asset-based (AUM) fees remain the core model (firm filings): The Bank of America 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says asset management fees are earned as a percentage of client AUM and generally range from 50 bps to 150 bps. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) reports advisory programs AUC of $1.1 trillion, with advisory programs' average AUC up 19%. It attributes its net revenue growth primarily to asset-based fee revenue and "the continued increase in investment of client dollars in advisory programs". On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CFO said a little bit over 20% of adviser-led flows are fee-based flows, and that this "still holds, if not growing".

Position - some rate compression visible from asset mix: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management 10-Q for the period ended 2026-06-30 (published August 2026) says asset management and related fees rose 6% in the quarter and 4% for the year-to-date period. It attributes this to higher average AUM and positive long-term net flows, "partially offset by lower average fee rates, reflecting a change in asset mix".

Position - flat, hourly and tiered alternatives sit alongside AUM pricing in firm disclosures: Raymond James's Wealth Advisory Services brochure (published 2026-09-14) says planning fees can be an hourly rate or fixed (flat) dollar fee. Investment consulting can be an hourly rate, a flat dollar fee, or a percentage of assets under advisement. Hourly fees are generally up to $400 per hour, and a percentage fee is not to exceed an annual rate of 2.25%. Morgan Stanley's advisory brochure (published 2026-11-04) states a wrap fee with a maximum annual asset-based Advisory Fee of 2.0%, plus SMA Sub-Manager Fees that generally range from 0.20% to 0.75%. Edward Jones's Advisory Solutions Fund Models fee (brochure published 2026-03-27) is asset-based, comprising a Program Fee and a Platform Fee, with higher-value accounts generally paying lower rates.

Position - firms say they would adapt pricing if clients move (management statements): On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Raymond James's CEO said the firm wants a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure". He said that if pricing evolves in the industry based on competitive pressures and client preferences, the firm would be "flexible and open to evolving", and that it reviews all pricing, fees and payout on an ongoing basis. On the same call, Schwab's CFO said Schwab's model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service. He added that if those preferences change, Schwab has a lot of flexibility.

Position - fee pressure is driven by competition and low-cost providers (firm risk factors): Edward Jones's 2025 10-K lists competition from robo-advisors and other lower-cost options, from firms offering discount services, and from major competitors that offer zero commissions on stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products. Bank of America's 2025 10-K cites pressure to provide products "on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies". It also cites competitors offering electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, which it says could cause pricing pressure. Morgan Stanley's 2025 10-K says it has experienced and may continue to experience pricing pressures as competitors reduce prices and fees or eliminate commissions. Schwab's 2025 10-K says it monitors pricing against competitors and periodically adjusts advisory fees, mutual fund and ETF expense ratios and commissions, and that reduced commissions or expense ratios could affect results.

Position - client demand for value, not lowest price (surveys and research): McKinsey (Feb 2025) reports that almost 80 percent of affluent households surveyed would rather pay a premium of 50 basis points or more for human advice than use a customized digital service priced at about ten basis points. It also reports that 29 percent are willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) says pricing is the top factor (48%) in final advisor selection but argues this is about demonstrating value for fees, not being cheapest.

Position - AI could compress fees on commoditized planning work (consultancy views, 2026): Deloitte (2026-05-20) says lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, while competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare. McKinsey (2026-04-08) describes markets questioning what clients pay for when AI makes once-invisible work fast and cheap. McKinsey says the advantage shifts toward firms that can prove and monetize outcomes. This sits alongside McKinsey's view that blanket fee cuts are unlikely.

Position - price transparency has itself driven competition (Raymond James): Raymond James's FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says that in fixed income and equity markets regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins. The firm says it believes pricing pressures will continue as some competitors seek market share by reducing fees, commissions or margins.

Position - transparency is delivered mainly through disclosure and conflict documentation (firm brochures): Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30, September 18, 2026 update) adds disclosure of new Support Fees, which it describes as a type of revenue sharing. It expects to begin receiving them on January 1, 2027, from third-party firms. It also adds disclosure of optional Data Analytics services and associated conflicts of interest. Merrill says it addresses compensation conflicts through brochure disclosure and by requiring advisors to recommend products that are in clients' best interest "considering cost". Schwab's brochure (published 2026-10-15) says its advisory fee may cost more or less than paying separately and that some reports show performance net of the fee while others show it gross. Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) says fund fees and expenses are embedded in the fund price and are not included in the Fee amount shown in account statements.

Regulatory enforcement on hidden or unfair charges (disclosed events): Morgan Stanley's brochure (published 2026-11-04) describes a May 12, 2020 SEC settlement order. The SEC found that, from at least October 2012 through June 2017, MSWM gave incomplete and inaccurate information in wrap fee program communications. As a result, some clients paid transaction-based charges that were not visible to them. A trade-press item (published 2026-10-16) reports a NASAA-led settlement over minimum commission practices. It says firms must certify that commission policies and supervisory procedures were revised to ensure charges are fair and reasonable. It lists earlier NASAA-led settlements with Raymond James (July 2023, $13 million) and with Edward Jones and others (June 2025, $9.3 million).

Regulatory framework referenced: A FINRA oversight document (published 2025-12-09) lists SEC staff guidance on Regulation Best Interest observations, conflicts of interest, account recommendations, and Form CRS disclosures. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K says it operates in a regulatory environment with ongoing change and that legislative and regulatory initiatives could affect how it markets products and interacts with clients.

Position - investors still do not clearly understand what they pay (FINRA Foundation, published 2025-12-04): Respondents most often mention account service fees (44 percent) and fees or commissions on trades (41 percent) as fees they pay. Of mutual fund or ETF owners, 45 percent report paying fund fees, 41 percent say they do not, and 13 percent do not know. In total, 20 percent of respondents do not think they pay fees of any kind and 18 percent do not know how much they pay. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) separately reports that 73% of participants consider fee transparency the most important trust factor.

Position - platform-level 'support' and data fees are being added or extended (Merrill): Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30) says Support Fees apply to third-party mutual funds, actively-managed ETFs and certain annuities, and to Style Manager Strategies. For actively-managed ETFs, Support Fees will be up to 0.10% annually of fund assets held in client accounts in the program. For annuities, they will be up to 0.15% on contract purchases. Merrill says Support Fees are a type of revenue sharing. Data Analytics fees are typically $125,000 to $860,000 per year, and $25,000 to $550,000 per year for passively-managed ETF data. Merrill also states it will charge the Support Fee only on underlying investments, so the same assets are not subject to more than one Support Fee.

Position - platform-level 'support' and data fees are being added or extended (Schwab): Schwab's investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) states that "New servicing fees will provide meaningful portion of ETF economics" and that discussions are already underway. Schwab's 10-K (published 2026-02-25) describes mutual fund and ETF service fees charged for services to Schwab and third-party funds, and order flow revenue from trade execution venues.

Position - platform-level fees are linked to zero commissions (trade-press attribution, Merrill coverage 2026-09-29): Trade press quotes sources saying the platform tolls at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions. It quotes consultant Greg O'Gara saying Merrill's disclosure acknowledges that support fees can limit the range of products available to clients. It also quotes the firm as saying it will have a financial incentive to make available and recommend products from third-party firms that pay fees for data analytics. Trade press reports Wells Fargo, UBS and Morgan Stanley charge their own data analytics fees.

Position - the debate over cash-sweep economics versus explicit fees is live: In the 1Q26 call (April 2026) a Wolfe Research analyst asked Raymond James whether it would consider platform fees if competitors pivot to a more fee-based model to reduce reliance on cash economics. Raymond James's FY2025 10-K and its fiscal Q2 2025 10-Q (August 2025) say its PCG results depend on how client cash is allocated across RJBDP, CIP and ESP. The 10-Q also says RJBDP fees decreased on a lower average third-party bank yield. Schwab's CFO said on the 1Q26 call that client cash is actively allocated, with transactional cash at about 4% of client assets. Merrill's brochure says there is no charge or fee for participation in its Cash Sweep Program and that advisors receive no additional compensation for sweep assets. Morgan Stanley's brochure says its Sweep Banks' lending and investing income is greater than fees earned from managing and distributing sweep-eligible money market funds.

Edward Jones's own product-level fee structure (brochure and 10-K): Edward Jones's Advisory Solutions Fund Models account pays an asset-based fee comprising a Program Fee and a Platform Fee. ETFs, affiliated and unaffiliated mutual funds in the account also carry internal fees and expenses described in each fund's prospectus. Edward Jones's 2025 10-K says other asset-based fee revenue consists of revenue sharing, fund adviser fees, cash solutions and Trust Co. fees.

adjacent.text: Trade press (Merrill coverage, published 2026-09-29) says that, per its sources, fee-based program fees at Merrill are comparable to RIA pricing at 1.00% and 1.40% of assets typically, and as high as 1.75%. It says transaction-based pricing for full-service brokers is a minimum commission of $75 or $0.04 per share, whichever is greater.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative; these figures are attributed to unnamed sources and are not in Merrill's own filings.

adjacent.text: Raymond James reports an average fee rate of 0.36% on $123.3 billion of total financial assets under management at June 30, 2026 (equity 0.58%, fixed income 0.29%, balanced 0.35%).
adjacent.differs_because: This is the Asset Management segment's average fee rate on its AUM, not a client-level advisory fee schedule or a trend over time.

gaps.what: Evidence on the adoption of subscription or retainer fee models beyond one 2023 survey (10% of teams retainer-oriented). The evidence shows no time series, no firm disclosure of subscription pricing, and nothing showing a shift in the mix of AUM, flat, hourly and subscription fees.
gaps.suggested_source: Industry compensation or fee-model benchmarking surveys over several years (e.g., Cerulli, Kitces, Schwab RIA Benchmarking), and firm investor-day disclosures on fee-model mix

gaps.what: No primary regulatory text (for example, SEC or FINRA rule releases on fee or cost disclosure) is in the evidence. Regulatory requirements appear only through firm filings, a FINRA list of staff guidance and enforcement items, so the direction of new fee-disclosure rules cannot be stated.
gaps.suggested_source: SEC and FINRA rule releases and exam priorities on Regulation Best Interest, Form CRS and fee/cost disclosure, and Form ADV Part 2A instructions

gaps.what: Quantified fund expense ratio trends and cash sweep rate changes at the firms asked about are not in the evidence. Cash sweep evidence is qualitative or limited to balances and fee direction at individual firms.
gaps.suggested_source: Fund-industry expense ratio studies (e.g., Morningstar, ICI) and firm 10-Q cash sweep and bank deposit account fee disclosures
